title: Birth, the cheese-box bass, and the first music he heard
summary: He says he was born in Louisiana, made a bass from a cheese box at about twelve, and recalls polkas and quadrilles and the old slow blues before St. Louis Blues.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Yeah, sure. I was born in Louisiana, yeah. I was born on Boilbun, between Scalmers and Cornelius. Oh, yes. And what year was that? 1817. I got my birthday if I can get it. 18... 17. Yes. And your birthday is, when will it be? On the 25th of Monday, 25th of this month. I was born in March. 87 years ago. 87 years ago. No, sir. I'm 87. Me, oh. Yes, that's what I mean. Yeah, that's what you mean. And what was the first kind of music you remember hearing around? Huh? What was the first kind of music you remember hearing in those days? Well, they had me, you're not talking to me, Poesie, you want me to explain to you? Yes. Well, me, I started to play with that bass I made. How old were you then? About 12 years old. 12 years old? Yes, sir. And? And I made the bass, and we had a band together. Guitar, bass, the little bass I made, and a man-lady. Give me. That's right. And how did you say you made the bass out of what? A cheese box. A cheese box. You don't have that in the mood. American cheese, they're all in pieces that come in a big box. Yeah. And I made a little neck, and like I told you, I went and bought some wire, and I made a little bow with wire, got some rosin put on there, and I learned that. You see, that was my first thought. Did they have many of those instruments here in the city then? They had the bass, but I wasn't positioned to buy them. Oh, I see. People had basses. Oh, they had basses, but I was natural at that time, my people didn't have them. They had sufficient, you know, to supply me to get them. When they did, they bought me a good one. When you were young, what kind of music did you hear around town? You know, I mean, before you started playing yourself, what were people playing around? Well, of course, I used to have polka. Polka. Muzuka. Cordrilles. Then, uh, a variety of dances that the white people dance. Varieties, dances. Cordrilles for color. Cordrilles for the colored people, they could dance brightly. That was the outfit. Just like what Cordrilles. Now, the colored people, the colored people, there's four on this side, four on this side. We played the Cordrilles, each of them danced, you know, swing and so on. You understand? Yes. Did they ever play blues then? Blues? Oh. They used to play blues, but they used to play real blues. They don't play no blues now. Right. What was the real blues? Huh? What was it like, the real blues? The real blues is tradition. That's St. Louis blues. It's a little bit of blues. But nobody can come to dig that either, I'll tell you that. The St. Louis blues, that comes a little after, before or after the other blues I'm going to tell you. Is it slow or fast? Slow. Real slow. And I can show you this time, I can dance and show you, I should dance it myself. That's about your hand. Huh? Yeah, that's right. I can do that. Well, knock it out for us. Just give us a beat huh? Yes. Jump On!
